title: First Guest
subtitle: Comparing Means Assignment · t-test, ANOVA, pairwise tests
story: The storm has passed and Fjellro is yours alone — for one more hour. Dagny Vold is already boarding the funicular far below, her friends beside her: the first guests of the day, and the last people you want to hand a flaw. Every bath must read true before they arrive. You start in the dim entry hall, where two summoning cords hang by the hidden stair — old servants' bells, though today they'll do something stranger. Thermometer in hand, you slip down to where the water is coldest.

done.title: The house reads true
done.body: Every bath, certified — cold plunge to hot spring, nothing out of balance and nothing for Dagny to find. Now to leave before she reaches the door.

escapeDone.title: First tracks
escapeDone.body: The five balance-candles hold their pattern and the gate to the piste clicks open. You step onto untouched snow just as the funicular crests the rise — flawless, and first. Let her follow.

coverPrompt: Minimalist stylised thumbnail poster of a single steaming Nordic hot-spring pool ringed by a few small candles at the foot of a great snowy mountain peak, one warm amber candle-glow reflected in the dark still water at dawn. Designed to read clearly as a small thumbnail: one bold, simple, high-contrast silhouette, iconic and uncluttered, minimal fine detail. Flat, limited palette: deep teal, icy blue, and one warm amber glow. Soft film grain, painterly but clean with simple geometric shapes. Strong negative space, single centred focal subject. No people, no text, no lettering, no logos. Square composition.

debrief.title: How Fjellro worked
debrief.intro: Every room asked the question a spa-keeper asks each morning: is this difference real, or just the wobble of water? You certified each bath by choosing the honest test for its data, and the springs by refusing to cry wolf on every pool after the storm. Here is how each room embodied the comparison of means.

Around the rest of the hall, iron candle-stands with warm candles, a low wooden bench, folded linen, hanging lanterns of amber glass. painterly, cinematic, serene and luxurious, warm amber candlelight with deep teal shadows, subtle film grain. No people, no lettering, no text, no captions, no UI.

entry.title: The cold plunge
entry.text: You leave the entry hall by the hidden stair and drop into the cold-plunge chamber, dark and close. Far down the mountain, Dagny's funicular has begun to climb. Two plunges here — and their candles are anything but alike.

rooms.debrief: Two cold plunges, one test. A t-test asks whether the gap between the two pools' mean temperatures is bigger than the noise within each; Shapiro and Levene both pass, so the t-test is the honest tool.

plannedHotspots.label: The plunge control panel
plannedHotspots.note: cold_plunge x temperature_C -> Shapiro/Levene pass -> t-test glacier vs fjord; fjord warmer, significant (p=9e-9)

question.prompt: The storm chilled the plunges overnight. Are the two cold plunges genuinely at different temperatures — and if so, which one is warmer?
options: Yes — a significant difference; plunge_fjord is the warmer of the two
No — the two plunges are not significantly different
Yes — but plunge_glacier is the warmer one
You can't test it — the data are non-normal, so no test applies
It's significant only if you skip the normality check first
They differ in salinity, but not in temperature
The variances are unequal, so the difference is untestable

feedback.correct: Certified — plunge_fjord runs warmer than plunge_glacier (about 11.3°C vs 9.4°C), a real difference. The candle above the passage lights.
wrong: Keep only bath_type == 'cold_plunge' and parameter == 'temperature_C', then compare the two baths.
Check the assumptions first: a Shapiro test (within each bath) and a Levene test (across the two) decide whether a t-test is fair here. Both pass — so the t-test is the honest, most powerful tool.
The two plunges do differ — look again at which bath's mean temperature is the higher one, not just whether they differ.

entry.title: The brine room
entry.text: The plunge is certified. Up a spiral stair into green light — pale pre-dawn now, falling through snow-banked windows. The funicular is higher, laughter drifting up. Two brine baths, and these candles look... matched.

rooms.debrief: The brine readings are skewed, so a t-test would lie. Reading that from the Shapiro/Levene checks and switching to the non-parametric Wilcox test is the lesson: pick the test the data has earned.

plannedHotspots.label: The brine control panel
plannedHotspots.note: saltwater x salinity_ppt -> Shapiro FAILS (skewed) -> Wilcox; brine_south saltier, significant (p=9e-4)

question.prompt: The brine baths spiked overnight and their salinity readings are jumpy. Is one brine bath genuinely over-salted — and which test is honest for data shaped like this?
options: A t-test — significant, brine_south is saltier
The two baths are not significantly different
A Wilcox test — significant, brine_south is saltier
A Wilcox test — significant, but brine_north is saltier
A Kruskal test — the right tool for these two groups
The data are normal, so a plain t-test is fine
The difference shows in dissolved solids, not salinity

feedback.correct: Certified — the salinity is skewed, so the non-parametric Wilcox test is the honest call, and it confirms brine_south is the saltier bath (median ~38 vs ~33 ppt).
wrong: Filter to bath_type == 'saltwater_bath' and parameter == 'salinity_ppt', then check normality before you pick a test.
The Shapiro test fails here — the salinity is right-skewed — so a t-test would mislead. Which two-group test makes no normality assumption?
A Kruskal test is for three or more groups; you have two. Reach for the two-group non-parametric test instead.

entry.title: The warm hall
entry.text: One brine bath was off; caught. A ladder lifts you into the warm hall, big windows blazing pale over the snowy peaks, sunrise close. The funicular nears the top. Four baths here — and one keeps different company than the rest.

rooms.debrief: Four baths, so a t-test won't do. ANOVA asks whether ANY of the four pH means differ; when it says yes, Tukey names WHICH one — the single drifted bath — without you fishing through every pair.

plannedHotspots.label: The warm-bath control panel
plannedHotspots.note: warm_bath x pH -> Shapiro/Levene pass -> ANOVA (sig) + Tukey -> warm_spruce is the odd bath

question.prompt: Four warm baths, and one of them has let its pH drift. Which single bath is out of line with the rest?
options: warm_birch
warm_spruce
warm_cedar
warm_pine
None of them — the four baths don't differ
All four baths differ from one another
Two baths are off, not one

feedback.correct: Certified — warm_spruce is the odd bath, its pH (~7.85) sitting well above the other three (~7.4). The Tukey follow-up pins it as the only one out of line.
wrong: Filter to bath_type == 'warm_bath' and parameter == 'pH'. With four baths, an ANOVA asks whether ANY of them differ.
ANOVA tells you something differs but not which — run a Tukey follow-up to name the single bath that stands apart.
Three of the baths sit together and agree; look for the one the follow-up flags against all the others.

rooms.title: The outdoor hot springs
rooms.technique: pairs of means — pairwise t + multiple-comparison correction (Holm)

authoring.scenePrompt: This is a panorama. A 360-degree view from the centre of the spa's outdoor hot springs at SUNRISE, open to a snowy mountain sky washed gold and rose, a broad stone deck, everything wrapping continuously all the way around so the left and right edges meet seamlessly. In the FOREGROUND, close at hand, are TWO clear pairs of soaking pools: the first pair's two pools are BOTH ringed with clusters of SMALL SHORT GREEN candles of matched size; the second pair has one pool ringed with TINY PURPLE candles and its partner ringed with MASSIVE TALL PURPLE candles, plainly different. Further off across the deck, reached by little stone paths, lie THREE MORE pairs of steaming pools, smaller with distance and clearly set apart from the two nearest pairs. Ahead, a weather-worn brass control panel on a stone plinth with a softly glowing console screen; beside it, a small pinned field-note under glass. Set into a low stone wall, a CLOSED heavy timber gate onward, and above it two candles — a GREEN one (unlit) and a PURPLE one (lit); on another side, an OPEN archway back down into the warm hall. painterly, cinematic, serene and triumphant, warm gold sunrise light and candle-amber, cool teal shadows, rising steam, subtle film grain. No people, no lettering, no text, no captions, no UI.

entry.title: The outdoor springs
entry.text: The warm hall reads true. The last passage opens onto cold sunrise air and the outdoor springs, steaming gold. Dagny is nearly at the door. Five pairs of pools in all — two close at hand, three further off along the paths.

rooms.debrief: Five pairs, five comparisons. Run that many tests and one will look significant by chance; the Holm correction strips out that false alarm, leaving only the pairs that truly differ — so you never 'fix' a spring that was fine.

plannedHotspots.label: The springs certification panel
plannedHotspots.note: hot_spring x temperature_C; pairwiseTTest(value ~ bath) grouped by `pair`, Holm -> ember/aurora/frost differ; slate flips OUT under correction; gale n.s.

question.prompt: The five spring pairs all wobble after the storm. Which pools' two tubs are TRULY mismatched in temperature, once you account for testing all five pairs at once?
options: All five pairs differ
None of the pairs differ
ember, aurora, frost and slate
ember, aurora and frost
ember and aurora only
slate and gale
frost and slate

feedback.correct: Certified — ember, aurora and frost are genuinely mismatched; slate and gale are not. Correcting for the five simultaneous tests strips out slate, which only looked off by chance.
wrong: Filter to bath_type == 'hot_spring' and parameter == 'temperature_C', then compare the two tubs within each pair — group by 'pair' and run the pairwise test.
You're running five comparisons at once. Uncorrected, one pair will look 'significant' by chance — apply the multiple-comparison correction the pairwise test offers.
Watch the borderline pair: it clears the line uncorrected but not once you adjust for the many tests. Don't 'fix' a spring that was actually fine.

plannedHotspots.label: The pinned field-note (hint)
plannedHotspots.body: A note in the last keeper's hand: “After a storm the pools all shiver — test enough of them and one is bound to look wrong when it isn't. Judge them together, not one at a time, and forgive the pool that only wavers by chance.”
plannedHotspots.note: boss hint: after a storm, the more pools you test the more likely one looks off by chance -> correct for multiple comparisons; does NOT name the answer

entry.title: The balance gate
entry.text: Every bath certified, honestly — nothing for Dagny to find. Sunrise breaks over the slopes; only the balance gate remains, its five candles dark. Go back, read each pair, and pull the right cords.

rooms.debrief: No console at the gate — just your eye. All morning you asked whether a difference was real; here you ask it of candlelight. A pair whose candles are plainly one massive, one tiny truly differ — light that colour; a pair whose candles all match does not — leave it dark. Recognising that, then finding each colour's cord a room behind, is the whole comparison made physical.

plannedHotspots.label: The balance gate — five colour+shape candles above the door
plannedHotspots.note: ESCAPE lock. 5 candles: vermillion/square, blue/circle, yellow/diamond, green/triangle, purple/star. CORRECT = vermillion, yellow, purple LIT (their candle-pairs DIFFER); blue, green DARK (their pairs MATCH). Set by the bell-cords in earlier rooms. -> escapeDone. ENGINE #16 (bell-pull) + #8 (state-gate) TO-BUILD; 'answer' records design intent.

rooms.designNote: ESCAPE — THE BALANCE GATE (ungraded, no codec; fires escapeDone). Five ceremonial candles above the final door, each a distinct COLOUR + SHAPE (colour-blind-safe: vermillion/square, blue/circle, yellow/diamond, green/triangle, purple/star), all initially UNLIT. The player recognises, by eye, which of the five candle-pairs seen in the earlier rooms DIFFER in size (vermillion, yellow, purple) vs MATCH (blue, green), then backtracks to pull each colour's cord (each sits one room before its pair) to LIGHT the differing three and leave the matched two dark. CORRECT = vermillion+yellow+purple lit. DATA-FREE (candles, not the water-chem). ENGINE #16 + #8 TO-BUILD. Colour never load-bearing alone — every colour carries a shape. New art.
